poiPAU-desc:
The East African Federation began in the landscapes of Tanzania and has grown remarkably since. {{poiPAU006|The road has been hard}}, but it reflects {{poiPAU005|the collective determination of East African nations}} to win sovereignty and freedom from outside influence. That pursuit is far older than the Great Mistake.

The vision behind it is {{poiPAU002|a united, centralized Africa}} in which {{poiPAU007|its many cultures and peoples}} live in harmony. {{poiPAU004|It has survived numerous trials}}. The vast and resource-rich Kongo region, and mega-corporations such as Morgan Industries, have posed formidable challenges to a unified continent. The struggle has not weakened, and there is still much to do to cast off the chains of historical oppression and dominance.

The Federation's core is the Azanian Union, together with Zambezia and Madagascar. The People's African Union around it also takes in Ethiopia, Oromia, Qafara, Somalia and South Sudan. Its rivals in the Bamako Compact and the Kimpwanza League watch it closely.

It is a journey fueled by the hope that a new, united African nation will rise from these trials, ready to defend its sovereignty and heritage not just for a century but for centuries to come. The Federation stands as a testament to a people determined to shape their own destiny.
poiPAU001-desc:
Avuncular, genial and affable, Jama Samatar wished to be addressed as Kubwa Mjomba—great uncle in Swahili—by those he both commanded and protected. Despite his seeming benevolence and absent-minded demeanor, he was an efficient administrator, an able diplomat, and ruthless when necessary. Detractors likened him to the village chieftains of the past, a throwback out of step with the world after the Great Mistake. Samatar was amused, and likely pleased.

He rose from the poverty and violence of the inundated streets of Hargeisa and joined the African Union's resurgent military forces, eventually reaching the rank of Major. For three decades he served in a variety of increasingly important military and civilian posts, rising steadily in both ability and influence. He overcame lingering tribal tensions by dealing with the polyglot cultures of Africa with both reverence and common sense.

Samatar proved just as efficient against any threat to the safety of those under his protection. Against nascent warlords, religious fanatics and local dictators, he either brought about an equitable peace or bludgeoned them into submission. He was never known as a military genius, but his troops were fiercely loyal to their great uncle and fought for his approval. He never lost a battle, took no credit for his victories, and saw them as lamentable necessities. Though not religious himself, he has been tolerant and accepting of others' religious traditions.
poiPAU002-desc:
The Federation is the direct successor state to the old African Union, which fell apart during the Congo Crisis of 2134. Although rife with nativist sentiments and anti-unification thought, it still clings to the hope of one day unifying the continent.

With each passing day, that possibility shifts into the realm of inevitability. The Federation wields the largest industrial base on the continent, the second largest land force in the world, and a rapidly modernizing society. The Pan-African Dream has not died, but flourished.
poiPAU003-desc:
The ABTBIA—or the African Board for Trade, Business, and other Internal Affairs—is the government body responsible for managing the economy. It has 50 seats, 40 elected on a regional level and 10 appointed by the President. There has been talk, mainly led by urban elites, of expanding it to 75 seats to better represent the Federation's diverse population.

The Board regulates public companies, sets financial standards and advises Parliament on relevant matters. All other oversight boards must file reports to the ABTBIA, and many have their directors appointed by an ABTBIA vote. Recently it has taken a special interest in heavy industry and the Pan-African infrastructure sector.
poiPAU004-desc:
From the Great Mistake to the Congo Crisis and the collapse of the African Union, the East African Federation still stands. It wields the largest industrial base on the continent, a rapidly modernizing society and the second-largest army in the world. Since the fall of the United States, the only superpower the world has known is the ailing People's Republic of China, and many in the Federation believe that the title is now theirs for the taking.

Manpower alone will not unite the continent or hold off a foreign invasion. The army has proven more than capable of subduing local warlords, but its older aircraft are long overdue for replacement, and its lands are littered with ancient tanks, some as old as the 20th century, kept as trophies, turned into tractors or fallen into bandit hands. The Federation is surrounded by hostiles: the Kimpwanza League to the west, unstable nations to the north, and the odd bandit warband squatting on its peripheries. An Orbital Military Institute, a small but advanced station where elite commanders would train in simulations and watch the conflicts below, was proposed decades ago and has yet to be built.
poiPAU005-desc:
The Pan-African Parliament holds many parties, but the major ones are surprisingly united in the goal of Pan-African nationhood. They disagree on its form and on where the priorities should lie, but that thread of unity has spared the Federation the infighting that has crippled so many other nations. Most subscribe in some way to Ujamaa, the cooperative ideal of fraternity by which the Federation has long governed itself.

The People's African Party of President Samatar Barre stands for the status quo: Pan-Africanism with socialist leanings and firm opposition to nativism, an Africa united politically, culturally and economically, protective of its citizens and sovereign abroad. Its years in office have been popular, though not without critics. Its direct rival is the Continental Popular Front of Walaalkaa Barre, the President's own brother. The Front is friendlier to nationalism while still rejecting nativism, would ease the rules on small businesses while holding corporations to account, and wants not a single Pan-African nation but a coalition in which every nation has a voice. It firmly rejects accusations of sympathy for the Kimpwanza League.

The Mbaba Mwana Waresa Foundation, named after a Zulu goddess of nature and led by Moyo Chengetai, courts the environmentalist vote, though it is far more interested in ecological engineering than in conservation. With farmers wracked by desertification and fishermen catching more plastic than fish, it has found an audience. The most unorthodox of the four, the Baadaye Mkali Party, takes its name from the bright future it promises, built on science, education and advanced technology in every sector.
poiPAU006-desc:
Whether it carries people without vehicles of their own or vast amounts of freight in a world after fossil fuels, the rail network is the backbone of {{poiPAU003|the Federation's economy}}, and every investment in it pays for itself. Railhubs at Addis Ababa and Kigali tie the Federation together, a line from Tanzania to Sudan has been proposed to bring the Sudanese closer, and the long-term goal is a network spanning all of Africa.

The Federation's heartland is Lake Nalubaale, once called Lake Victoria. Its ample water and successful anti-pollution efforts have drawn huge numbers of settlers to its shores, and its transport struggles to keep up. Kampala International Airport, formerly Entebbe, is long overdue for an overhaul. Along the coasts, efforts to restore the ocean have had some success against the pollution, overfishing and warming that ruined the communities that once lived from the sea.
poiPAU007-desc: With more than 3,000 ethnic groups and 2,000 languages on the continent, a united Africa depends on understanding them. The African Cultural Academy of Languages, Art and Nationhood promotes the education, recognition and use of African cultures, and has begun exploring affordable AI-assisted translation. For the Federation it is the cultural half of the Pan-African project, and its funding is a matter of state.
